draft.title: Intertextual references in images
card: Intertextuality is when one text refers to another text. A visual text, such as a poster, ad or cartoon, can borrow from a well-known image.
The borrowed image might be a famous painting, a film poster or a photograph. Creators copy its pose, layout or colours so viewers recognise it.
Viewers who recognise the original bring its meaning to the new image. This adds ideas without the creator having to explain them.
A viewer who does not know the original can still read the new image. They may miss some of the added meaning.
draft.remember: Borrowing a familiar image lets a new image carry the old one's meaning.

a.q: What makes a poster an intertextual reference to a famous painting?
opts: It copies the painting's look so viewers link the two
It uses bright colours to attract attention
It has a caption that names the artist
It shows a different subject in a new style
a.why: Intertextuality depends on the new image deliberately echoing a known one, so viewers link them. Bright colours and a new style do not point to another text, and a caption alone does not make the image echo anything.
a.clue: Think about what viewers must recognise.

b.q: A council's recycling poster shows a girl holding a bin in the same pose and layout as a famous portrait. What is the most likely reason for this choice?
opts: To bring the portrait's fame and meaning to the poster
To show that the portrait was painted long ago
To prove the poster is cheap to print
To make the poster hard for viewers to understand
b.why: Copying a well-known image lets viewers carry its meaning over to the new message. Showing the age of the portrait is not the creator's purpose here. Making the poster hard to understand works against a council's aim.
b.clue: Ask what viewers gain by recognising the original.

a.best: It copies the painting's look so viewers link the two

b.best: To bring the portrait's fame and meaning to the poster

problems.detail: The wrong options are implausible, especially 'To make the poster hard for viewers to understand' and 'To prove the poster is cheap to print'. A student could pick the right answer without knowing the idea, so the question is too easy for Year 8.
The right option is the longest. It is also the only one that echoes the card's wording ('copy... so viewers recognise it'), so it stands out from the others.

proposal.title: Intertextual references in images
card: Intertextuality is when one text refers to another text. A visual text, such as a poster, ad or cartoon, can borrow from a well-known image.
The borrowed image might be a famous painting, a film poster or a photograph. Creators copy its pose, layout or colours on purpose so viewers recognise it.
Viewers who recognise the original bring its meaning to the new image. This adds ideas without the creator having to explain them.
A viewer who does not know the original can still read the new image. They may miss some of the added meaning.
proposal.remember: Borrowing a familiar image lets a new image carry the old one's meaning.

a.q: What makes a poster an intertextual reference to a famous painting?
opts: It deliberately imitates how the painting looks
It is printed at the same size as the painting
It shares a theme with the painting by chance
It was made in the same year as the painting
a.why: An intertextual reference is a deliberate borrowing that viewers can recognise, such as a copied pose or layout. A theme shared by chance is tempting, but nothing was borrowed on purpose, so viewers are not being pointed to the painting.
a.clue: Is the link to the painting made on purpose?

b.q: A council's recycling poster shows a girl holding a bin in the same pose and layout as a famous portrait. What is the most likely reason for this choice?
opts: To let viewers carry the portrait's meaning to the message
To make viewers think the portrait's artist made it
To teach viewers the history of the famous portrait
To make sure only art fans can understand the message
b.why: Copying a well-known image lets viewers who recognise it bring its meaning to the new message. It does not limit the poster to art fans, because viewers who do not know the portrait can still read it. They may just miss some of the added meaning.
b.clue: What do viewers gain when they recognise the original?

b.best: To let viewers carry the portrait's meaning to the message
